components.text: The decisive demand is whether consciousness is ontologically prior rather than dependent on physical processes.
Whether conscious experience is ontologically prior to the physical processes investigated by science.
The decisive demand is whether neural computational dependence exhausts the fact of conscious awareness.
Whether neural computational dependence exhausts the fact of directly known conscious awareness.
The decisive demand is whether an extra fact of consciousness remains after cognitive capacities are explained.
The broader idealist claim requires consciousness to be more than the capacities studied by cognitive science.
Whether an extra fact of consciousness must be added beyond all observable cognitive capacities.
Whether consciousness must be treated as an ontologically additional basis rather than a constituted capacity.
The decisive demand is whether brain dependence shows production or only mediated access to consciousness.
Whether neural dependence should be interpreted as production of consciousness rather than access to it.
Whether an access model supplies a coherent extra-consciousness alternative to functional production.
The earlier account requires explaining why unconscious brain computation cannot realize temporal ownership and continuity.
The extra-subject proposal also bears on the objection to positing entities beyond explained capacities.
Whether unconscious brain computation can constitute temporally unified ownership, memory, and anticipation.
Whether positing a persisting subject adds an unnecessary entity beyond cognitive capacities.
The decisive demand is whether brain use requires a separate inner user or persisting non-brain subject.
Whether using the brain requires a separate persisting inner subject that serves as its user.
Whether consciousness includes an additional fact beyond evolved functional organization.
Whether the brain is merely an access device used by consciousness.
The decisive demand is whether an evolved brain interface preserves genuine purposes rather than merely representing them.
Whether a brain described as an evolved interface can possess genuine purposes rather than merely simulate them.
Whether purposeless neural and physical processes can preserve experienced aims as causally genuine.
Whether functional capacities exhaust the purposive features attributed to conscious agents.
The decisive demand is whether a purposeless process can generate genuine system-level purposes.
Whether a purposeless physical process can generate genuine purposes at the level of organisms and artifacts.
The decisive demand is whether selection-based functions explain present thoughts referring to and causing unrealized future outcomes.
Whether evolutionary organization can explain present representations that guide action toward future outcomes.
Whether an evolved interface can possess causally efficacious future-directed representations.
The decisive demand is whether discovery and improvement require values to exist outside natural human practices.
Whether genuine moral discovery requires values that exist independently of human construction and nature.
Whether evolved predictive capacities can generate discoveries and improve goal-directed practices.
The earlier challenge asks how future-directed ideas can causally guide action within a physical description.
Whether responsibility and agency require a nonphysical value-bearing chooser rather than autonomous control capacities.
Whether physically realized systems can possess genuine goal-directed control and purposes.
Whether practical abilities can guide future-directed conduct without indeterministic causation.
The decisive demand is whether autonomy suffices without genuinely alternative futures controlled by the agent.
Whether autonomy and robust abilities suffice for culpability without genuinely open alternative futures.
The decisive demand is whether influences on an autonomous person amount to determination or leave genuine agent choice.
Whether character, education, and prior causes determine action or merely influence a deciding agent.
Whether acquired moral practices can shape choice without exhausting personal agency.
The decisive demand is whether nondetermination adds agent control rather than merely introducing randomness.
The controlled-alternatives account requires explaining why an open future improves trustworthy agency.
Whether removing determination adds agent control rather than an uncontrolled random difference.
Whether genuine alternative futures produced by indeterminacy increase responsibility or trustworthiness.
The earlier move's decisive demand concerns whether an agent chooses without being fully determined by formative influences.
Whether personal continuity requires a persisting subject rather than materially vulnerable organization.
Whether moral agency depends on a continuing chooser beyond reproducible physical information.
The decisive demand is whether informational persistence or reproducibility amounts to survival of the relevant person or meaningful entity.
Whether stored or reproducible information is sufficient for continued existence of the person or meaningful work.
Whether informational organization alone constitutes the experienced subject.
The earlier demand asks why stored informational structure is insufficient for survival of a conscious or meaningful entity.
Whether naturalistic explanation necessarily eliminates genuine value, meaning, beauty, love, and wonder.
Whether naturalistic explanation can preserve genuine purpose rather than declare it illusory.
Whether naturalistic explanation preserves responsibility-relevant human significance.
Whether naturalism can explain mortality and the desire for immortality without reducing their importance.
The decisive demand is whether asserted naturalistic adequacy is complete or remains a forward-looking research commitment.
Whether the asserted adequacy of naturalistic accounts is already established or remains unfinished work.
Whether the naturalistic consciousness program is complete enough to warrant its comprehensive claims.
Whether evolutionary explanation already covers every disputed aspect of purpose.
The decisive demand is whether confidence in unfinished naturalism is an unsupported faith commitment.
Whether confidence in future naturalistic explanation is unsupported faith or evidence-based methodological trust.
The decisive demand is whether naturalism must reduce every personal-level explanation to a physical-level description.
Whether failure of microphysical description to replace higher-level explanation demonstrates metaphysical irreducibility.
Whether absence of value terms from an atomic catalogue places value outside natural reality.
Whether purposive explanation at a higher level requires purposive fundamental components.
Whether nonreplaceability by a physical description entails an additional nonphysical fact.
The decisive demand is whether personal-level value and self explanations are merely autonomous levels or reveal irreducible realities.
The broader naturalistic claim must preserve the reality and importance of value-directed personal conduct.
Whether value-directed personal explanation is fully preserved if the continuing deciding self is treated as a brain-based illusion.
Whether naturalism preserves what is most important in value-directed personal life.
Whether the continuing deciding self is merely an evolved user illusion.
Whether conduct explained by pursued value retains genuine normative significance.
